title: Seek the city's peace (Jeremiah 29:4–11)
hookLine: to exiles: build houses, plant gardens, pray for the city you're in

cards: A letter arrives in Babylon. It has come hundreds of miles from Jerusalem, carried by royal messengers.
The people reading it are exiles: priests, craftsmen, families, taken from home along with King Jeconiah, living now in the capital of the empire that conquered them. And they're restless.
Some prophets are telling them not to unpack; in Jerusalem, one has promised it will all be over within two years. The letter is from Jeremiah.
Surely he'll tell them how to hold on, how to resist, how soon they'll be free.

teach.b: Unpack, says Jeremiah. In the King James Bible: "Build ye houses, and dwell in them; and plant gardens, and eat the fruit of them." Marry.
Have children. Let your children marry. Grow there, don't shrink.

Then the line that must have stunned them: "And seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives, and pray unto the LORD for it: for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace."
Pray for Babylon, the city whose army marched you away from home.
The word for peace is shalom, and it means much more than no war: wholeness, welfare, everything as it should be. Enough food, safe streets, healthy families, right relationships.
Seek Babylon's shalom, because yours is tied up in it. Jeremiah also warns them not to listen to the prophets promising a quick return.
It will be seventy years, he says, a lifetime.

teach.h: SEEK THE PEACE OF THE CITY.
teach.b: Then comes a verse you may have seen on coffee mugs: "For I know the thoughts that I think toward you, saith the LORD, thoughts of peace, and not of evil, to give you an expected end." Thoughts of shalom.

It's worth knowing its first setting: written to a whole community, to be kept through seventy years of exile, most of whom would not live to see the return. A promise for the long haul, not the next week.

Jewish communities in the centuries since have often prayed for the welfare of the countries they lived in, and many Christians have read this letter as a guide for living faithfully in any place that isn't quite home.

how: Many churches pray each Sunday for their city, nation and leaders, and Jeremiah 29:7 is often cited as the reason; in many synagogues a prayer for the welfare of the government is said on the Sabbath.

o: peace as wholeness: welfare, with nothing missing
a quiet feeling of calm inside yourself
a short break in fighting between armies

games.q: what's inside the letter — tap the pairs.

s: Jeremiah told the exiles to resist Babylon and prepare to leave
he told them to build, plant, marry, and seek the city's peace.
Jeremiah 29:11 was first written to a whole community in exile
a long-haul promise, kept through seventy years, not a personal forecast.
shalom just means the absence of war
it means wholeness, welfare: everything being as it should.

games.q: you've been carried off to the city of your conquerors. a letter from home arrives. what does it tell you to do?
o: don't unpack: you'll be home in two years.
build houses, plant gardens, and pray for the city.
keep to yourselves and wait it out.
games.why: "seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives, and pray unto the LORD for it." pray for Babylon.

practice: Picture the place where you live now, whether it feels like home or not: its streets, its schools, its people who annoy you, its mayor or council, whether or not you voted for them.
Then picture one place in it that isn't whole, a closed shop, a shelter, a struggling school, a lonely street, and hold it gently, wishing it shalom. If you pray, you can pray for your city by name.

wordCard.voice: Shalom. Peace as wholeness and welfare: what Jeremiah told exiles to seek and pray for, even in the city that took them captive.

orig.note: Hebrew: peace, wholeness, welfare. still a greeting in Hebrew today.

carryVoice: Your line: pray for your city. Its shalom and yours are tied together. Day four hundred seventy-five.
